senses.definition: Lopsided between two sides, such as a small possible loss against a much bigger gain.
senses.caution: It says nothing about how likely something is. Use it only if you can say which side is bigger and by roughly how much, because investors will ask for both numbers.
senses.example: The pilot is asymmetric: worst case we lose a quarter of one team's time, best case we retire two vendors.

cues.text: You are pitching a small pilot to a sponsor. The cost is capped at one quarter of a team's time and the payoff, if it lands, is retiring two suppliers, and you want the word for that shape.
An investment committee asks why you would take a chance that will probably fail, and your answer is about the size of the two outcomes rather than the odds.
In a negotiation the vendor knows your budget and you do not know their costs, and you want a word for that imbalance.
A friend asks whether to send a speculative application for a job they almost certainly will not get. It costs them an evening and it could change their decade.
You are talking your partner out of skipping travel insurance to save forty pounds on a trip that has already cost thousands.

distractors: Harder or larger than the person asking has assumed it would be.
Big enough to matter, said of an amount, a change, or a piece of work.
A range with no natural joints in it, where the cases shade into one another.
A structure where everyone can be watched at any moment and nobody knows when they are.
Training signal a machine can check for itself rather than a person having to judge it.
